entries.title: How could people travel the Inca road without modern machines?
entries.answer: The Inca connected many existing routes and built new roads through western South America. Builders used stone steps or walls where a path climbed a slope. At some deep river crossings, bridges made from woven fibers gave travelers a way across. Runners could carry a message from one stopping point to the next, and llamas could carry loads. The network mattered because its builders found different ways to fit a road to mountains, valleys, and dry places.
facts: Some communities still maintain traditional bridges along former Inca routes.

entries.title: How did a city grow on a lake?
entries.answer: Tenochtitlan was the Aztec capital. It grew on islands and shallow land in a lake where Mexico City stands today. Roads built above the water connected it with the shore. Canoes could carry people and loads along canals. The nearby market at Tlatelolco brought many kinds of goods and people together. Water made travel possible as well as difficult, so people used roads, canals, and gardens in different ways. The city fell to Spanish forces and their Indigenous allies in 1521.
facts: The main Aztec temple area is called the Templo Mayor.

entries.title: How did Aksum become a powerful trading kingdom?
entries.answer: Aksum was a center of an ancient kingdom in what is now northern Ethiopia. Its routes linked highland towns with ports and the wider trade of the Red Sea. Merchants could carry goods across warm lowlands and over the water toward Arabia and the Mediterranean world. Aksumite rulers made coins and raised tall carved stone monuments. Some monuments still stand where they were set up, so archaeologists can study what their size and position tell us about the people who built them.
facts: Some carved monuments at Aksum look like tall buildings with several floors.

entries.title: How did Babylon become a great ancient city?
entries.answer: Babylon stood on the Euphrates River in what is now Iraq. It was a center of power more than once. Under the Neo-Babylonian rulers, it had tall city walls and a grand road for ceremonies. One entrance called the Ishtar Gate was decorated with pictures of animals in glazed brick. The walls directed people entering the city, while the gate showed what its builders could do. Ruins and objects give us a clearer picture of Babylon than legends alone.
facts: Babylon was the capital of the Neo-Babylonian Empire from 626 to 539 BCE.

entries.title: How did Carthage become a sea power?
entries.answer: Carthage began as a settlement founded by Phoenician seafarers on the North African shore, near modern Tunis. A harbor close to routes across the Mediterranean made it a useful place to trade. From Carthage, ships could connect towns on both the African and European sides of the sea. As Carthage grew, it became powerful in its own right and fought Rome. Rome destroyed the older city in 146 BCE, then later built a Roman city at the same site.
facts: The remains of Carthage are in present-day Tunisia.

entries.title: How did people live in ancient Egypt?
entries.answer: In ancient Egypt, much of daily life followed the Nile River. Flooding once left rich mud across nearby fields. People farmed that land and carried water to their crops in channels. They caught fish and used river plants to make a writing material called papyrus. Villages and cities depended on the work of farmers, builders, craft workers, and people who could read and write. Over thousands of years, Egyptian rulers and beliefs changed, so a family in one period could live differently from a family many centuries later.

sections.heading: How we know
sections.text: Pictures in tombs show some jobs and tools. Surviving objects and written records give other clues. Some people left far more evidence than others.

facts: The Nile supplied water and useful plants.
Papyrus can mean the river plant or a material made from it.

entries.title: How did Roman aqueducts carry water?
entries.answer: A Roman aqueduct carried water from a source, such as a spring, toward a place people needed it. Builders gave the water channel a gentle downhill slope so gravity kept the water moving. When the channel reached a valley, a bridge could hold it high enough to keep that slope. The stone arches you see in some pictures are supports. The water flowed in a channel near the top. Other parts of a long journey might run through a tunnel or along the ground.

sections.heading: A bridge that carried water
sections.text: The Pont du Gard, in present-day France, carried an aqueduct across the Gardon River. The full aqueduct ran roughly 50 kilometers, or 31 miles.

facts: An aqueduct can include a bridge, a tunnel, or a covered channel.
The Pont du Gard supplied water to the ancient Roman city now called Nîmes.

entries.title: How did Rome govern itself before its emperors?
entries.answer: For several centuries Rome called itself a republic. Instead of having one king with the job for life, Rome used elected officials with shorter terms. Two officials called consuls usually held the top job at the same time. The Senate had great influence, and different groups of citizens voted in assemblies. Women, enslaved people, and many other people who lived under Roman rule did not have those voting rights. After years of conflict, Augustus gained power and Rome entered the age of emperors.
facts: The Roman Senate continued to meet even after emperors began to rule.

entries.title: How did Rome govern lands far beyond Italy?
entries.answer: Augustus gained control of Rome and its lands more than two thousand years ago. Rome’s empire stretched across large parts of Europe, western Asia, and northern Africa. Governors and other officials helped run provinces. Roads and ports made it easier to send messages, goods, and officials between places. People spoke many languages and kept different local customs. Some cities copied Roman building styles, while each region’s older traditions continued to shape daily life. The empire changed over the centuries as its rulers and borders changed.
facts: Augustus is usually counted as Rome’s first emperor.

entries.title: How did the ancient Maya organize their cities?
entries.answer: Ancient Maya people built cities across parts of what are now Mexico and Central America. Each city and the lands around it could have its own ruler. Rulers built temples and palaces around open spaces and had writers record dates and events. Neighboring cities might trade or form friendships, then compete or fight at other times. Cities changed as people moved, and some lost their importance. Maya people, languages, and traditions are still part of life in the region today.
facts: Tikal was among the large ancient Maya cities.

entries.title: How did the ancient Persian Empire govern faraway lands?
entries.answer: The Achaemenid kings ruled an empire that stretched from Egypt and western Asia toward the Indus region. A king could not visit every town to decide what should happen there. Officials governed regions and answered to the king. The empire included people with many languages and local customs. Carvings from Persepolis show groups bringing objects from different lands. These pictures show how the rulers wanted people to see the empire, not everything that daily life there was like.
facts: Cyrus the Great founded the Achaemenid Empire in the sixth century BCE.

entries.title: How did the Inca rule across the Andes?
entries.answer: The Inca Empire stretched along the Andes of western South America before Spanish conquest. Its rulers governed from Cusco and linked many communities with roads. Travelers crossed steep valleys, mountain slopes, and drier regions. Workers built stairs, walls, and bridges that fit different places. Storehouses along routes held goods for people working or traveling on behalf of the empire. The roads could help people move, but the growing empire also expected communities it ruled to provide work and supplies.
facts: The empire included places in several of today’s South American countries.

entries.title: How did the Qin form one Chinese empire?
entries.answer: Before the Qin empire, several powerful states competed for land in China. The Qin ruler defeated the others and called himself the First Emperor in 221 BCE. His officials put common rules for writing and measures in use across the empire. Having the same kinds of measures helped officials compare goods from different places. The Qin dynasty ended soon after the First Emperor’s lifetime, but later rulers kept the idea of governing wide regions from one center.
facts: The name Qin is usually said like “chin” in English.

entries.title: How do we know about the Shang dynasty?
entries.answer: The Shang dynasty ruled parts of northern China more than three thousand years ago. Its craftspeople made large bronze containers with carefully shaped patterns. Archaeologists also found animal bones and turtle shells with writing carved on them. Some record questions that rulers asked about the weather or harvests. Old stories about the Shang were written down much later. The objects are especially useful because people made and used them at the time those rulers lived.
facts: Carved Shang bones and shells preserve some of the earliest known Chinese writing.

entries.title: What changed in China during the Han dynasty?
entries.answer: The Han dynasty ruled for about four hundred years, with an interruption, after the Qin. Government officers kept written records and helped run provinces far from the main cities. Some rulers sent envoys west, and contacts with Central Asia grew. People in different regions exchanged goods such as silk and horses. The historian Sima Qian wrote a wide account of earlier rulers and events. Later readers could use works like his to learn how people thought about the past.
facts: The Han began in the late third century BCE and ended in 220 CE.

entries.title: What do city streets tell us about the Indus civilization?
entries.answer: The Indus civilization grew in South Asia thousands of years ago. Today archaeologists study cities such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa to learn how people there lived. At Mohenjo-daro, some streets followed long straight lines, and many buildings used bricks. Covered drains carried water away from some homes and streets. Small carved seals show pictures of animals and lines of signs. Archaeologists can describe these objects and streets, but there is no agreed reading of the signs yet.
facts: Sites belonging to the Indus civilization lie in parts of present-day Pakistan and India.

entries.title: What do the walls of Mycenae tell us?
entries.answer: Mycenae was a wealthy center on the Greek mainland in the late Bronze Age. Builders used very large stones in its walls. Above the main gate, a carving shows two lionlike animals standing on either side of a column. The settlement had a palace and important graves. Records at several Mycenaean sites used marks called Linear B, an early way to write Greek. The walls and writing help us learn about leaders who lived centuries before the best-known Greek city-states.
facts: A similar fortified site called Tiryns is near Mycenae.

entries.title: What made Uruk one of the earliest cities?
entries.answer: Uruk grew in southern Mesopotamia more than five thousand years ago. Thousands of people could live near one another there. Large mud-brick buildings took more work to plan and build than a single family could handle. People who grew food worked alongside people who made pots, traded, or kept accounts. Some of the oldest tablets found at Uruk count goods. Details such as those help archaeologists see a city working, even though they cannot hear what people said in its streets.
facts: Uruk covered a much larger area than most nearby settlements around 3200 BCE.

entries.title: What was ancient Greece?
entries.answer: Ancient Greece included many communities around the sea. Some cities and the area around each city formed a separate government. We call these places city-states. Athens and Sparta were two powerful examples. Many communities shared parts of their language and religion, and athletes traveled to meet at festivals. They could also disagree and fight wars. Objects such as painted pots and buildings with carved stone can show how people worked, played sports, and honored their gods.
facts: Athens and Sparta had separate governments.
Ancient Greeks gathered for games at Olympia.

entries.title: What was the city of Ur?
entries.answer: Ur was a large city in southern Mesopotamia. One of its best-known buildings was a ziggurat with stepped levels that rose above the flat ground. Three stairways rose toward the entrance on the front. The surviving outer brickwork helps archaeologists study how older builders made a huge structure from layers of material. Graves and everyday objects at Ur offer other clues about life there. A tall building tells us about organized labor, while a small object can tell us about someone’s work or habits.
facts: A ruler named Ur-Nammu began the great ziggurat at Ur about four thousand years ago.

entries.title: What was the Kingdom of Kush?
entries.answer: Kush was a kingdom farther up the Nile from Egypt, in what is now Sudan. People there built towns, temples, and burial places. At times Kush and Egypt traded, and at other times their rulers fought for land. Kushite kings even ruled Egypt for a period. Later, Meroë became an important Kushite center. Its small, steep pyramids and decorated chapels show how builders used ideas from the Nile region and made buildings with their own shapes and details.
facts: The Nile runs through lands that once belonged to both the Kingdom of Kush and ancient Egypt.

entries.title: Who built the large palaces of ancient Crete?
entries.answer: The people we call Minoans lived on Crete thousands of years ago. They built large groups of rooms around open courts at places such as Knossos. The buildings held spaces for storage and work, so they were more than homes for wealthy people. Craftspeople painted walls and made objects that could be traded across the sea. Some of their writing survives. Archaeologists compare the buildings and objects to understand a society that left few written texts most people can read today.
facts: The name “Minoan” comes from Minos, a king in Greek stories.

entries.title: Why are there clay soldiers near an emperor’s tomb?
entries.answer: The First Emperor of Qin had a huge burial site built near what is now Xi’an. People shaped and fired clay figures of soldiers, horses, and other members of his court. Rows of these figures stood in pits outside the mound holding his tomb. Many figures are close to life-size. Their different hair, faces, and armor help visitors imagine an army made up of individual people. Workers digging a well found pieces of the figures in 1974.
facts: Archaeologists have found thousands of clay figures at the burial complex, along with other objects.

entries.title: Why can people still see streets and houses at Pompeii?
entries.answer: Pompeii was a town near Mount Vesuvius in what is now Italy. In 79 CE the volcano erupted, and ash and other material covered the town. The buried rooms, walls, and streets stayed hidden for centuries. By uncovering them, researchers found buildings and everyday objects that might otherwise have been lost. A shop counter or a painted wall can give a clue about how people worked or spent their time. Archaeologists still take care when uncovering and protecting the fragile remains.
facts: Vesuvius also buried the nearby town of Herculaneum.

entries.title: Why did ancient Romans build so many roads?
entries.answer: Roads tied ancient Rome to places across its growing territory. A good road made it easier to move travelers, soldiers, animals, and goods over land. One well-known example is the Appian Way, which started at Rome and was later extended to the port city of Brindisi. Parts were paved with stone. A road also needed structures such as bridges and places to get through steep land. Some sections of ancient roads remain visible today, giving us a look at how people traveled long before cars.
facts: Construction of the Appian Way began in 312 BCE.
The Appian Way connected Rome to the southeast of what is now Italy.

entries.title: Why did cities grow between the Tigris and Euphrates?
entries.answer: Mesopotamia was a region around the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. In its drier southern lands, people dug channels to bring river water to their fields. Farming could support people who did other work, such as potters, builders, and traders. Some settlements grew into cities. Mud from the plains could be shaped into bricks and dried, so people built with a material they could find close to home. The region included many different peoples and governments over thousands of years.
facts: Much of ancient Mesopotamia lies in present-day Iraq.

entries.title: Why did Maya people use more than one calendar?
entries.answer: Maya people kept track of several cycles of time. One calendar counted 365 days. Another repeated after 260 days and was important for religious life. A day could have a place in both cycles at once, a little like having both a weekday and a date on your calendar. A separate system called the Long Count recorded dates over much longer times. Multiple systems let people record familiar cycles and also describe events far back in time.
facts: The same pairing of dates in the 260-day and 365-day cycles returns after about 52 of the longer years.

entries.title: Why was the Great Pyramid built?
entries.answer: The Great Pyramid at Giza was built as a tomb for Khufu, a ruler of ancient Egypt. It rises from a broad, square base and has four sides that slope toward the top. Inside are stone passages and chambers. The pyramid is the largest of three famous pyramids at Giza. It stands near other structures that belonged to a royal burial site, including smaller pyramids and tombs. Egyptologists, people who study ancient Egypt, still ask exactly how builders moved and lifted all that stone.
facts: Khufu was also known as Cheops in Greek.
The Great Pyramid is more than 4,000 years old.

entries.title: Why were Hammurabi’s laws carved in stone?
entries.answer: Hammurabi was a king of Babylon who had rulings carved into a tall dark stone almost four thousand years ago. The small wedge marks give examples of disputes and punishments. Some deal with such problems as an injury or a building that falls. The rules sometimes treated people differently depending on their place in society. At the top, an image shows Hammurabi before a god linked with justice. The tall carving made a statement about the king’s duty to rule.
facts: The writing on the stone is in cuneiform, and the monument is kept at the Louvre.
